specAnchors.text: understand, in terms of changes in oxidation number, the following reactions of the halogens: i oxidation reactions with Group 1 and 2 metals ii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with water and the use of chlorine in water treatment iii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to form bleach iv the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with hot alkali v reactions analogous to those specified above

primer.text: Halogens duel for electrons, and the stronger fighter always wins. This note sets out the displacement rule, works the ionic equations that expose the electron transfer, and reads the colour evidence - aqueous shades and organic-layer purples - that turns test-tube observations into halide identification.

modules.title: The displacement ladder of the halogens
modules.opening: Drop chlorine water into bromide solution and the chlorine robs bromide of its place. Displacement reactions are the reactivity ladder made visible: a halogen higher in Group 7 pushes a lower one out of its salt, and every such contest is a redox reaction.
keyPoints: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide.
Chlorine displaces bromine from bromide solution and iodine from iodide solution.
Bromine displaces iodine from iodide solution, but cannot touch chloride.
Each displacement is a redox reaction: the displaced halogen is oxidised while the displacing halogen is reduced.
Spectator ions such as sodium or potassium are removed to write the ionic equation.

low.restatement: The higher halogen wins the electron tug-of-war: chlorine takes bromide's electron, bromine takes iodide's, but nothing lower can take from anything higher.
low.analogy: Like a stronger magnet pulling pins off a weaker magnet - the pins (electrons) always move towards the stronger pull, never backwards.
low.examPointer: Write the ionic equation with the spectator ions removed, e.g. Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2, and label the oxidation-number changes for full marks.

medium.restatement: The displacing halogen drops from oxidation number 0 to -1 (reduction) while the displaced halide climbs from -1 to 0 (oxidation), so electron transfer is explicit in the ionic equation.
medium.analogy: Two climbers swap positions on a ladder: one descends two rungs (gains electrons), the other climbs two rungs (loses them), and the ladder's total is unchanged.
medium.examPointer: Quote the electron ledger, not just colour change, when the question says 'show that this is a redox reaction'.

modules.title: Observing displacements: aqueous colours and the organic layer
modules.opening: Displacement announces itself in colour: yellow-orange for bromine, brown for iodine in water, and a dramatic purple iodine shade once an organic solvent collects the halogen. This lesson converts those observations into positive halide identification.
keyPoints: Chlorine solution added to potassium bromide gives a yellow-orange colour as bromine forms.
Chlorine solution added to potassium iodide gives a brown colour in water, and iodine appears purple in an organic solvent layer.
An organic solvent such as cyclohexane concentrates the halogen products, making the colour changes easier to see.
Bromine displacing iodine likewise gives brown in water and purple in the organic layer.

low.restatement: Each successful displacement paints its product colour: bromine yellow-orange, iodine brown in water but purple when shaken into an organic layer, where halogens dissolve more readily.
low.analogy: The organic solvent is a spotlight that gathers the scattered halogen into one vivid  puddle of colour for the eye to judge.
low.examPointer: Quote both the aqueous colour and the organic-layer colour when identifying the halide - examiners award the mark for the paired observations.

medium.restatement: The halogen products differ in solubility preference: they favour the organic phase, so adding cyclohexane extracts the halogen and sharpens the diagnostic colour. The colour itself tracks the identity of the displaced halogen, not the reagent.
medium.analogy: Like separating oil droplets from water: the halogen gathers into its preferred layer and the colour intensifies enough to read unambiguously.
medium.examPointer: Do not confuse bromine's aqueous brown with iodine's purple organic layer - mislabelled colours lose the identification mark.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which a more reactive halogen pushes a less reactive halogen out of its halide solution.
An ion present in the mixture whose oxidation number is unchanged, so it is omitted from the ionic equation.
A balanced equation showing only the species that actually change oxidation state during the reaction.
